factors.name: R&D intensity
factors.why: Research spending per dollar of sales.

factors.name: Cash conversion
factors.why: Operating cash flow minus net income, per dollar of assets. High means profits are backed by cash.

factors.name: Revenue growth
factors.why: Sales this year vs last year.

factors.name: Operating margin
factors.why: Operating profit per dollar of sales.

factors.name: Net margin
factors.why: Profit kept from each dollar of sales.

factors.name: Return on assets
factors.why: Profit per dollar of everything the company owns.

factors.name: Asset growth
factors.why: How fast the balance sheet grew. Fast growers have tended to disappoint.

factors.name: Return on equity
factors.why: Profit per dollar of shareholder money.

factors.name: Free cash flow margin
factors.why: Cash left after investment per dollar of sales.

factors.name: Share count change
factors.why: Rising means dilution; falling means buybacks.

factors.name: Leverage
factors.why: Liabilities as a share of assets.

factors.name: Gross profitability
factors.why: Gross profit per dollar of assets.

factors.name: Margin change
factors.why: Net margin this year minus last year.

factors.name: Earnings growth
factors.why: Net income this year vs last year (only when last year was profitable).

verdict: 5 of 14 filing factors separated winners from losers in most years: R&D intensity (high is better, 20.8% a year), Cash conversion (high is better, 8.6% a year), Revenue growth (high is better, 8.0% a year), Operating margin (low is better, 20.1% a year), Net margin (low is better, 16.5% a year).
caveats: Tested only on companies in the S&P 500 today, so companies that failed or were dropped are missing and results look better than they were. Annual reports only. Returns are measured for 12 months from the day after each filing, against the average stock.
